report:
**Conclusion:** The claim is plausible but too strong as stated. Evidence does **not** establish that simply being vegetarian reliably increases life expectancy versus eating meat.

The best evidence is observational (cohort studies), so diet is entangled with smoking, body weight, exercise, income, healthcare use, and—critically—the quality of both vegetarian and meat-containing diets. It measures death rates over follow-up, not lifespan directly, and cannot prove causation.

Findings are mixed. In the Adventist Health Study-2, vegetarian patterns were associated with lower all-cause mortality, especially among men. However, that population has unusually health-conscious lifestyles, which limits generalization.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23836264/

Conversely, a systematic review/meta-analysis found lower ischemic-heart-disease mortality among vegetarians but **no effect on all-cause mortality**; it rated the certainty low.  
https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34611632/

British prospective-study evidence likewise found no clear all-cause mortality advantage for vegetarians compared with comparable nonvegetarians.  
https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4691673/

There is good reason to reduce certain meats: IARC classifies processed meat as carcinogenic to humans and red meat as probably carcinogenic, based chiefly on cancer evidence. That supports limiting processed/red meat, but does not demonstrate that all meat consumption shortens life or that vegetarianism itself lengthens it.  
https://www.iarc.who.int/featured-news/media-centre-iarc-news-redmeat/

**Bottom line:** A well-planned vegetarian diet can support health and may reduce heart-disease risk, particularly when it replaces processed/red meat with minimally processed plant foods. But current evidence cannot confidently say vegetarianism, by itself, increases life expectancy relative to a high-quality omnivorous diet.
